My friend was employed by a company on Grade Level 9, with an agreed monthly salary of $1,070.

However, when the salary department processed his first salary, they mistakenly placed him on Grade Level 10, which attracted a monthly salary of $1,890.

For six consecutive months, he received $1,890 every month without any complaint or warning from HR or the finance department.

He assumed the company had made an adjustment to his salary based on his qualifications and experience.

Then, one Monday morning, everything changed.

He received an official email from HR informing him that an internal salary audit had uncovered an error in his payment records.

According to the email, he had been mistakenly paid on Grade Level 10 instead of Grade Level 9 for six months.

The company calculated the difference as $820 monthly, bringing the total overpayment to $4,920.

HR instructed him to refund the entire amount within 30 days or agree to deductions from his future salaries.

He immediately requested a meeting with HR.

Employee: I don’t understand why I’m being asked to refund money that your own department approved and paid into my account for six months.

HR: We understand your concern, but your employment letter clearly states Grade Level 9. The salary department mistakenly entered Grade Level 10.

Employee: And who prepared the payroll?

HR: The salary department.

Employee: Who approved the payments?

HR: Finance and management.

Employee: So, for six months, everybody approved the payments, but now I’m the one being held responsible?

HR: We are not blaming you. We simply need to recover the excess payment.

Employee: I never requested a salary upgrade. I never altered my employment records. I received exactly what your company paid me.

HR insisted that the company had a responsibility to recover the money.
Someone just STOLE the most valuable company in the world, worth four TRILLION dollars, in broad daylight.

IShowSpeed just won Streamer of the Year for the third year in a row, walked up to the mic in Los Angeles, and gave his whole speech in Indonesian.

He's from Cincinnati. The reason goes back to one night in Jakarta in 2024, when he was 19 and started crying on camera.

He was on his Southeast Asia tour, walking around Jakarta live, and the viewer count kept climbing until 1,043,028 people were watching at the same time. No English-language streamer had ever done that. He'd set his personal record in Thailand about a week earlier, and Jakarta beat it by around 70%.

So last night, holding the trophy, he gave the moment back to them.

He opened with "Aku mulai dari nol." I started from zero. Anyone who's ever pulled into a gas station in Indonesia knows that line, because it's what the Pertamina attendant says before almost every fill-up to show you the pump starts at zero.

The money side of this is what I keep thinking about.

YouTube pays creators way less for an Indonesian view than an American one. Roughly a sixth, depending on the category. If you ran Speed's channel off a spreadsheet, you'd keep him home chasing American viewers.

He kept getting on planes instead. Seven countries in Southeast Asia in 2024, and more than 20 countries this year, including Kenya, Nigeria and Egypt back in January. An ad buyer calls those places cheap traffic, and he treated every one like a home game.

His channel had about 30 million subscribers the week he landed in Jakarta. It has 62.3 million now.

Turns out a country that feels seen gives you something ad rates can't measure. A million people show up live, all at once, and that kind of crowd is what lands you a Super Bowl ad and a World Cup tour across the US.

So he spent the biggest speech of his year on the viewers who earn him the least per view, and 32 million new subscribers later, it's hard to argue with the math.

Many of you still think soldiers die like heroes in clean, decisive moments. This footage from Height 105-106 shows the actual pattern: short, brutal close encounters in trenches and treelines where both sides take heavy losses in seconds. The foreign volunteers (US, Canadian and others) who went into Alfa and Bravo did not stroll in as invincible veterans; they closed with the enemy under fire, cleared positions, and finished the fight at arm’s length. Officials on both sides will call the dead martyrs or heroes. That is a cliché that softens reality for people who have never watched these frames.

This is not the Middle East style of engagement most Western veterans trained for. Iraq and Afghanistan experience does not automatically transfer. Standard training and past tours do not prepare you for the density of fires, the constant drone threat, and the pure infantry meat-grinder of these European fields. You can be a veteran of Kandahar or Fallujah and still not last long if you trust only old skills. As the Afghan proverb says: everyone is gang until they go to Kandahar. The ones who actually went into those trenches found out quickly that talk and prior service do not change the arithmetic of short-range killing. Most of the fallen on either side were not dying as storybook heroes. They were simply there when the next burst of fire arrived.
